name: The Three Forks sample depot
short_status: Intact and uncollected: ten sealed titanium tubes Perseverance laid on the floor of Jezero Crater between 21 December 2022 and 28 January 2023. As of 3 September 2026 no mission is scheduled to retrieve them.
tagline: NASA · United States · Sample depot · 2023 · Multipolar Mars Operating
stats: sealed tubes lying on the ground in Jezero Crater
to build and document the depot, per NASA's robotic operations chief engineer
missions scheduled to collect them as of September 2026

facts.label: What it is
facts.value: A backup cache of ten sealed sample tubes lying loose on the Martian surface at a spot called Three Forks, on flat ground near the base of Jezero Crater's fan-shaped ancient river delta. NASA describes it as the first sample depot built on another world.

facts.label: Why it exists
facts.value: Through its first seven rock sampling sites and one regolith site, Perseverance drilled twin cores. One of each pair stayed in the rover, which was to be the primary way of handing samples to a Mars Sample Return lander. The other went to the depot, to be collected by two Sample Recovery Helicopters if the rover could not make the rendezvous.

facts.label: First tube down
facts.value: 21 December 2022, sol 653. An igneous core informally named Malay, drilled on 31 January 2022 at South Séítah. The Sampling and Caching System took almost an hour to fetch it from the rover's belly, viewed it one last time with the internal CacheCam, and dropped it about 89 cm (3 feet) onto a chosen patch of ground.

facts.label: Last tube down
facts.value: 28 January 2023, sol 690. It was the witness tube sealed at the Amalik sampling site, the only one of Perseverance's witness tubes placed in the depot. JPL's release says confirmation reached mission controllers around 5 p.m. PST (8 p.m. EST) on Sunday 29 January, one day after the drop.

facts.label: The ten tubes
facts.value: Named, in the order NASA lists them by distance from the rover in its February 2023 depot panorama: Amalik (witness), Atsah and Skyland, then Bearwallow, Coulettes, Montdenier, Crosswind Lake and Roubion, then Mageik and Malay.

facts.label: What is inside them
facts.value: Seven rock cores (Montdenier, Coulettes, Malay and Atsah are igneous; Skyland, Bearwallow and Mageik are sedimentary), one regolith sample (Crosswind Lake), one atmospheric sample (Roubion) and one witness tube (Amalik). NASA's own summary of the set is one sample from each pair taken so far, plus one atmospheric sample and one witness tube.

facts.label: The odd one out
facts.value: Roubion, catalogued as tube 1 and as the mission's atmospheric sample, is the tube from the failed first coring attempt on sol 164 (6 August 2021). The corer reached its full commanded 7 cm depth, the tube was transferred and sealed correctly, and then the volume measurement came back empty: the rock had crumbled and no core survived. The sealed tube holds Martian air.

facts.label: Tube dimensions
facts.value: Each tube is about 18 cm (7 inches) long and about 2 cm across, and they are titanium. NASA's depot map page gives the tube and glove (adapter) combination as 18.6 cm, and says the team mapped each one precisely so the samples could be found even if covered with dust.

facts.label: Layout
facts.value: An intricate zigzag, with the tubes 5 to 15 metres (15 to 50 feet) apart so that each could be reached safely, a spacing given in JPL's depot-completion release. The rover drove roughly 8 to 22 metres between drop zones. NASA's chief engineer for robotic operations, Vandi Verma, put the whole job at 42 sols, 207.93 metres of driving, ten dropped tubes and 4,000 images.

facts.label: Why that shape
facts.value: Helicopter access drove the geometry. A circle of radius 5.5 metres around each drop had to be free of hazards for a Sample Recovery Helicopter, the tube had to land within 70 to 95 cm of that circle's centre, and rocks about 2 cm across counted as hazards for a 2.3 kg rotorcraft with small wheels and a gripper. The whole depot had to sit 200 to 700 metres flight distance from a plausible lander site. Nothing could block Perseverance's high-gain antenna during a drop, and the rover had to keep a return route through the depot in case a tube needed re-imaging or toppling.

facts.label: Invisible from orbit
facts.value: An 18 cm tube is far below what any camera at Mars can resolve. HiRISE, the sharpest, shot Jezero at about 29 cm per pixel, map-projected to 25 cm, and its own caption for the Perseverance landing frame states that objects about 88 cm across are resolved. Every published picture of the depot was taken by Perseverance itself, which is why NASA's depot map records each tube's position: the tubes have to be findable even under dust.

facts.label: Share of the collection
facts.value: NASA's sample catalogue, last updated 20 June 2026 and read on 3 September 2026, lists 30 of Perseverance's 38 sample tubes and 3 of its 5 witness tubes as used, which is 33 of the 43 tubes it carried. Ten of those 33 are at Three Forks. At an AGU briefing in December 2025, reported by SpaceNews, the project said six empty tubes remained and two filled tubes were deliberately left unsealed so their contents could be swapped.

facts.label: Mars Sample Return defunded
facts.value: The conference report on the fiscal 2026 appropriations minibus, released 5 January 2026, states: "As proposed in the budget, the agreement does not support the existing Mars Sample Return (MSR) program." It instead directs $110 million to a Mars Future Missions account to preserve radar, spectroscopy, entry, descent and landing and related technologies. The House passed the bill 397 to 28 on 8 January and the Senate 82 to 15 on 15 January. (SpaceNews's report of the Senate vote says 16 January, but that report was published on the evening of 15 January, so the date appears to be a slip; The Planetary Society gives 15 January.) President Trump signed it into law on 23 January 2026, a date for which The Planetary Society is our only source.

facts.label: The European half
facts.value: ESA's contribution was the Earth Return Orbiter, awarded to Airbus Defence and Space under a 491 million euro contract in October 2020. After the US vote, ESA's Director of Human and Robotic Exploration Daniel Neuenschwander said Mars Sample Return was "currently not planned to be continued", and following the 345th ESA Council meeting he said member states had "asked for the cancellation of the Earth Return Orbiter mission", with talks under way with Airbus about reusing hardware such as the electric propulsion system.

facts.label: Who owns the tubes now
facts.value: Legally, the United States does. Article VIII of the 1967 Outer Space Treaty gives a launching state continuing jurisdiction and control over objects it launches, wherever they end up, and space law has no concept of abandonment. Another state could physically collect the tubes but that would not transfer ownership; whether the obligation to return a recovered space object extends to the material inside it is not settled.

facts.label: Is the rover still working
facts.value: Yes. NASA published a HiRISE image on 24 June 2026 showing Perseverance as a green speck west of Jezero on 13 June 2026, the day before it passed a marathon of driving (42.195 km) on sol 1890, five years and four months in; Opportunity took eleven years and two months to cover the same distance. Perseverance's own waypoint file, read on 3 September 2026, records 700 waypoints, sol 1965 and 45.11 km (it gave sol 1955 and 44.98 km on 23 August 2026, and 694 waypoints, sol 1947 and 44.97 km on 16 August 2026). The depot lies about 9.9 km behind the rover in a straight line, and about 2.4 km from the landing site. Nothing in NASA's published plans has it going back.

timeline: Sol 164: Perseverance's first coring attempt, at a target called Roubion, drills to full depth but the tube comes back empty. Sealed anyway, it becomes the mission's atmospheric sample and eventually the depot's oddest occupant.
Sol 653: the igneous core Malay is dropped about 89 cm onto the surface at Three Forks, the first tube of what NASA calls the first sample depot built on another world.
Sol 690: the tenth and last tube, the Amalik witness tube, goes down. WATSON photographs it on the ground.
Confirmation that the depot is complete reaches controllers at JPL around 5 p.m. PST, according to JPL's release, which is itself datelined 28 January. NASA's pages do not resolve the one-day gap.
Sol 693: Perseverance takes a 368-image Mastcam-Z panorama of the finished depot, with the nearest tube 3 metres away and the farthest about 60 metres off, then drives away up the delta.
Vandi Verma, chief engineer for robotic operations at JPL, publishes the reasoning behind the depot's shape: helicopter landing circles, antenna sight lines and a rover route back through the field.
After cost and schedule overruns, NASA announces it will study two alternative Mars Sample Return architectures through mid-2026.

At an American Geophysical Union briefing, deputy project manager Steve Lee says Perseverance is "really in excellent shape" and capable of many more years, while conceding there are few public updates on how or whether the samples will ever be returned.

The fiscal 2026 appropriations minibus is released. Its report states that the agreement does not support the existing Mars Sample Return program, and moves $110 million into a Mars Future Missions account instead.
The bill is signed into law after passing the House 397 to 28 on 8 January and the Senate 82 to 15. The campaign that the Three Forks depot was built for no longer has a budget line.
ESA confirms that member states have asked for the cancellation of the Earth Return Orbiter, the European spacecraft that was to catch the samples in Mars orbit and carry them home.

Four US senators ask appropriators for at least $400 million for Mars Future Missions in fiscal 2027, warning of "severe and irreversible harm" to the ability to land on Mars. Lockheed Martin says it still stands behind a plan to return the samples for under $3 billion.

images.caption: PIA25738, a photomontage of ten WATSON images, each showing one sealed titanium sample tube lying on the Martian surface shortly after Perseverance set it down at Three Forks between 21 December 2022 and 28 January 2023. From the left: Malay, Mageik, Crosswind Lake, Roubion, Coulettes, Montdenier, Bearwallow, Skyland, Atsah and Amalik.

PIA25340, the WATSON camera on Perseverance's robotic arm photographing the tenth and final tube of the Three Forks depot on the ground on 28 January 2023, sol 690. It is the witness tube sealed at the Amalik sampling site, the only witness tube placed in the depot.

PIA25736, Perseverance's Mastcam-Z portrait of the finished sample depot taken on 31 January 2023, sol 693, stitched from 368 individual frames, with the colour adjusted to approximate what the surface would look like to the human eye. The full photojournal original is 29705 by 20033 pixels and about 77 MB; this is NASA's own smaller rendition of the same image.

PIA25682, NASA's map of the Three Forks depot, with a labelled circle marking where each of the ten tubes was deployed in the zigzag pattern, the tubes set roughly 5 to 15 m apart so a recovery vehicle could reach them safely.
PIA25663, a composite of stitched WATSON frames showing the first sample tube Perseverance deposited on the Martian surface on 21 December 2022, sol 653, the igneous core informally named Malay.
